extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (esp. Locke/early modern epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of how the mind forms ideas of number, space, duration, and infinity, plus a survey of 'simple modes' (motion, sounds, colours, tastes) and why some modes receive names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number measures all Measurables.
rubrics_metrics.description: Number is what the mind uses to measure all things that are measurable, principally expansion (space) and duration (time); our idea of infinity as applied to these derives from the 'endless addition' characteristic of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that number supplies an inexhaustible stock for mental addition; the 'endless addition or addibility' of numbers gives the clearest and most distinct idea of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity, in its original Intention, attributed to Space, Duration, and Number.
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite and infinite are seen as modes of quantity and primarily attributed to things with parts (space, duration, number). When applied to God, infinity is conceived with reference to duration and ubiquity and figuratively to other inexhaustible attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish primary attribution (space/duration/number) from figurative attributions to divine attributes; warns about the limits of our conceptions when applied to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Idea of Finite easily got.
rubrics_metrics.description: Our idea of finite arises straightforwardly from obvious portions of extension and ordinary bounded periods of time (hours, days, years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts the ease of acquiring the idea of finite with the difficulty of forming boundless ideas of eternity and immensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How we come by the Idea of Infinity.
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind repeats any stated length or duration and by endless addition reaches an idea of infinity; repetition and the power to continue adding give rise to the notion of infinite space or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses examples of repeating units (feet, miles, years) and doubling to show how the mind is led to conceive an endless progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our Idea of Space boundless.
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the mind can always conceive more extension (and because motion requires empty space), we are apt to think of space as actually boundless — the imagination finds no end to space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from the possibility of motion into void spaces and from the uniformity of the idea of empty space to the impression that space is infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: And so of Duration.
rubrics_metrics.description: By repeating any length of duration we form the idea of eternity; the mind's capacity for endless repetition yields the idea of infinite duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes having an idea of eternity from proving the actual existence of an eternal being; points to later discussion elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why other Ideas are not capable of Infinity.
rubrics_metrics.description: Only ideas that have parts and can be increased by adding smaller parts (space, duration, number) give rise to infinity; qualitative ideas like whiteness or sweetness cannot be augmented by repetition in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that degrees (whiteness, sweetness) unify rather than add, so repetition does not produce an endless enlarging idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between infinity of Space, and Space infinite.
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the idea of 'infinity' as an endless growing idea produced by mental repetition from the idea of a determinate quantity 'a space infinite' which would require the mind to have a completed view of all repeated parts — a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns of confusion when joining 'infinite' to a determinate quantity; calls for careful distinction between an endless process and a completed infinite magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: We have no Idea of infinite Space (positive idea).
rubrics_metrics.description: Although we can form the idea of the infinity of number clearly, we lack a coherent positive idea of an actually infinite space because any positive idea of space is terminated and thus incompatible with endless progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the contrast with numbers to show the absurdity of a completed infinite; stresses that our positive ideas are always finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number affords us the clearest Idea of Infinity.
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all ideas, number best furnishes the mind with the clearest notion of infinity because it allows distinct repeated ideas kept ordered by number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that when contemplating infinity in space or time we actually use numerical repetitions (millions of miles/years) to approach the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Conceptions of the Infinity of Number contrasted with those of Duration and Expansion.
rubrics_metrics.description: Number is often thought of as having one terminating end (unit) while addition proceeds indefinitely; duration and extension are imagined as lines extended both ways, producing different intuitions about eternity and immensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how eternity is conceived by applying numerical extension both forwards and backwards (a parte post and a parte ante).

rubrics_metrics.name: How we conceive the Infinity of Space.
rubrics_metrics.description: We imagine ourselves at the center and extend indeterminable lines in all directions by continuously adding spatial units by number, yielding the idea of immensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel to conception of eternity; uses spatial examples (yard, mile, diameter) and unlimited numerical addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite Divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.description: Because thought cannot reach an ultimate indivisibility of matter, thought is led to an apparent infinity via division (fractions) as well as addition; this is another form of the mind's endless progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the analogy between endless division and endless numerical addition; neither yields a positive idea of an actually infinite magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: No positive Idea of Infinity.
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no positive (complete, determinate) idea of an actual infinite number, space, or duration; what we call 'infinite' is the mind's power to continue adding, not a comprehensively represented whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes a test: ask if one could add to one's idea of the infinite — the ability to add shows the idea is not posited as a completed infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How we cannot have a positive idea of infinity in Quantity.
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that treat the negation of an end as positive are mistaken; beginnings and ends in duration are more than bare negations, and a so-called positive infinite conceals negative, indeterminate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques attempts to make 'infinite' into a positive determinate idea by highlighting contradictions (e.g., adding infinites should be impossible if truly completed).

rubrics_metrics.name: What is positive, what negative, in our Idea of infinite.
rubrics_metrics.description: When imagining infinity we first assemble many positive ideas (large numbers of years/miles) but the remainder beyond those positives is obscure and negative — an indeterminate 'still greater' rather than a clear comprehensive magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes: (1) clear positive idea of so much, (2) clear comparative idea of greater, (3) the idea of 'so much greater as cannot be comprehended' which is negative and indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: We have no positive Idea of an infinite Duration.
rubrics_metrics.description: If duration necessarily entails succession, then eternity must be an infinite succession of moments; since we cannot posit a positive completed infinite number of moments, we lack a positive idea of eternal duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects attempts to rescue a positive idea via punctum stans (a timeless instant) and insists on the improbability of a comprehensible positive eternity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No complete Idea of Eternal Being.
rubrics_metrics.description: Although reason may lead us to posit an eternal Being with no beginning, the negation of a beginning does not provide a positive, comprehensive idea of infinity; attempts to form such an idea leave us at a loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges belief in an eternal being but distinguishes that belief from having a clear positive idea of eternity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No positive Idea of infinite Space.
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous to duration: any positive idea of space is bounded; the part beyond our positive comprehension remains obscure; thus we lack a positive idea of infinite space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses examples of divisibility and measurement to show humans cannot form a completed idea of infinite smallness or largeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some think they have a positive Idea of Eternity, and not of infinite Space.
rubrics_metrics.description: Some believe they can positively conceive eternity (because of theological commitments) but not infinite space; Locke argues this is inconsistent because idea-formation depends on sensation/reflection, and the idea of infinite space need not imply infinite matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that belief in God's eternity doesn't make the idea more positive; both space and duration ideas derive from repeated finite measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supposed positive Ideas of Infinity, cause of Mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusions and paradoxes in discourses of infinity signal that our ideas of infinity are defective and disproportionate to our finite capacities; people who treat infinite as a completed positive magnitude fall into perplexities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urges caution and humility: allow those convinced they have positive ideas to keep them, but recognizes many paradoxes arise from such mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: All these are modes of Ideas got from Sensation and Reflection.
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas of duration, space, number, infinity, and their complex modes all originate from sensation and reflection; even our idea of infinity ultimately comes from these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admits mathematicians might have advanced ways to form ideas of infinity but maintains that initial ideas arise from sensory experience and internal reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other simple Modes (overview).
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond number/space/duration, there are many simple modes derived from sensation: motion, sounds, colours, tastes and smells, etc., which the mind combines into complex ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces subsequent subsections enumerating examples (motion, sounds, colours, tastes) and sets up treatment of complex ideas built from simple sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple modes of motion.
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like slide, roll, tumble, walk, creep, run, dance, leap, skip, etc., correspond to distinct modifications of motion; modes of motion are analogous to modes of extension and often complex (involving space and time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that swift and slow are modifications measured by distances of time and space combined; motion modes are complex ideas combining time and space with motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Sounds.
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate words and musical tunes are different modifications of sound; the mind can form the idea of a tune by reflecting on combinations of notes even when no sound is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out the musician's ability to form internal (imagined) complex ideas of sequences of sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Colours.
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours present many modes (shades, degrees) and are often taken as part of mixed modes that include figure (e.g., beauty, rainbow), so many colour modes belong with mixed ideas rather than simple enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why pure colour modes are less frequently assembled into named species because figure often participates (painting, weaving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Tastes.
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounded tastes and smells are modes composed of simple sensory ideas, but they often lack specific names and are left to the reader's experience rather than formal enumeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes that because many taste/smell modes have no names, they are less catalogued in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some simple Modes have no Names.
rubrics_metrics.description: Many simple modes that differ only by small degrees are not given distinct names — either because measures are lacking to distinguish them or because fine distinctions are not generally useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that simple modes like unity, duration, motion, power, thinking have been more often named and modified into complex ideas because of human concern with actions and relations among people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why some Modes have, and others have not, Names.
rubrics_metrics.description: Human practical concerns (communication about people and actions) drove the naming of many action-related complex ideas; utility determined which modes were carefully distinguished and named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests that naming arose where distinguishing ideas made social communication easier and more necessary.
